spec.cue: The view is grainy and wide, with ultraviolet flowers and flicker that the bee's eyes make visible.

cpd.note: honeybee workers resolve about 0.26 cycles per degree

fovea.note: no record gives a sharper middle for bees

fall.note: the app's guess for how sharpness falls with light; no record gives a curve for bees

uvBlue.note: the ultraviolet channel is shown in the blue channel, as the bee's colour mapping requires

glow.note: movement glows so that flicker is visible

rate.note: time runs slower to suggest a faster flicker rate

living.note: no extra weight for living movement

topoA.note: by analogy with the house cat

BEE.note: peaks near 340, 436 and 556 nm, from Apis mellifera records (Land 2012 gives 344, 436, 556; Kolyfetis 2025 gives about 340 nm)

field.name: squeeze
field.note: the wide field is squeezed toward the view's width

gaze.name: strip
gaze.note: the view scans in quick jumps

steady.name: lock
steady.note: the picture holds steady between jumps

saccade.note: quick head turns; 40 degrees and 4 frames are the app's choice

rows: A honeybee worker can resolve gratings of about 0.26 cycles per degree, roughly 1/230 of a person's detail.
Bees see close to 300 degrees around them, with the edges seen coarsely.
Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, peaking in the ultraviolet near 340 nm, in the blue near 436 nm and in the green near 556 nm.
Bumblebees turn their heads in quick jumps of 5 to 60 degrees, lasting 45 to 135 milliseconds, then hold gaze between turns.
The blur, the glow of movement, the brightness and the slowed time are the app's own choices, chosen to show how a bee's view differs. No record gives their values.
